\chapter{Afternoon}
\label{ch:hi-afternoon}
\hlchaptermodality{30}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say afternoon in Hindi using \hi{दोपहर} in its modern, widened sense.}

Say \hi{दोपहर} \hi{में} for 'in the afternoon' — the Chapter 17 word doing a wider job than its etymology promises.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[dopahar]{\hi{दोपहर} — the same word, a wider job than its etymology promised}

\label{lesson:HI-C30-dopahar-widened}



\begin{quote}
You already know \hi{दोपहर} means \textquotedblleft{}noon\textquotedblright{} — two pahars after sunrise, precisely. This lesson's honest twist is that the word doesn't stay that precise in everyday use.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{दोपहर} — same word, a broader modern meaning}
\textbf{\hi{दोपहर}} (\textbf{dopahar}) is the exact word you met in Chapter 17, still literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{two pahars}\textquotedblright{} (traditional \textasciitilde{}3-hour watches, counted from sunrise) — but in \textbf{modern, everyday Hindi}, it no longer points only at that precise midday instant. Say \textbf{\hi{दोपहर} \hi{में}} (\emph{dopahar mein}, \textquotedblleft{}in the dopahar\textquotedblright{}) to arrange a meeting, and you're pointing at a stretch of time — roughly \textbf{noon through late afternoon} — not a single moment. The historical etymology gave the word a very specific target (the end of the second daytime \emph{pahar}); everyday usage has since widened that target into the general block of time most languages call \textquotedblleft{}the afternoon.\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Be honest: etymology and modern meaning have drifted apart}
This is worth sitting with: \hi{दोपहर}'s \textbf{literal} story still holds up the way Chapter 17 described it — \textquotedblleft{}two pahars,\textquotedblright{} with noon falling around the end of the second — though, as that lesson itself noted, treat the exact pahar-count as the general shape of the story rather than a precisely dated fact. Either way, the \textbf{word's job} in the language has moved on well past that etymology. This kind of drift — a word for one precise instant loosening into a name for a whole surrounding stretch of time — isn't unique to Hindi, but here it's especially visible because Chapter 17 showed you exactly how tight the original math was.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dopahar\textquotedblright{} — the same word from Chapter 17, \textquotedblleft{}two pahars\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}dopahar mein\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}in the afternoon,\textquotedblright{} a modern, widened usage
  \item the honest twist — the etymology stayed precise; the word's actual job widened past it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \hi{दोपहर} a new word, or the same one from Chapter 17? (\textbf{The same word} — \textquotedblleft{}two pahars.\textquotedblright{}) Does modern Hindi use \hi{दोपहर} to mean only the exact instant of noon? (\textbf{No} — it's widened to cover the whole afternoon, roughly noon through late afternoon.) Has \hi{दोपहर}'s etymology itself changed to match this wider modern use? (\textbf{No} — the etymology still points precisely at noon; only the word's everyday job has widened.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ja]{\hi{ज} — a letter you have been reading without being taught}

\label{lesson:HI-S132-letter-ja}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \textbf{\hi{ए}} — does it sit on a consonant or stand alone?

This next one is not new to your eye. It is new to your hand.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{ज}}
\textbf{\hi{ज}} — \emph{ja}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item an open left hook curling clockwise around the lower bowl and continuing through the middle bar
  \item a top-to-bottom right stem
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Script: where it has been hiding}
You have been reading this letter for a long time without anyone stopping to name it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{जी}} — the respect-marker in \textbf{\hi{जी} \hi{हाँ}}
  \item \textbf{\hi{जनवरी}} — January, and \textbf{\hi{जून}} and \textbf{\hi{जुलाई}} after it
\end{itemize}

That is worth saying out loud rather than passing over. A letter can appear on every other page and still never be \textbf{taught}, because the words that carry it were introduced for their meanings and the shapes inside them were left to look after themselves.

\textbf{Seeing a shape often is not the same as being shown it.} The first gives you a guess; the second gives you the letter.

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{ज}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} start at the open upper-left tip, sweep down and clockwise around the lower bowl, then rise through the inner shoulder and continue right along the middle bar to the right-stem junction without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and draw the right stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 2.} The pen comes up 2 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
Verified three-stroke teaching form fitted to the bundled printed outline; everyday handwriting may divide the hook and bar differently.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-\hi{ज}-order.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 10 May 2009.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words and find \hi{ज} in each one
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\hi{जी}  ·  \hi{जनवरी}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{ज} three times, saying \emph{ja} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Say it:} how many times the pen comes up (two)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What sound does \textbf{\hi{ज}} carry? (\emph{ja}.) Name one word you already say that contains it. Had you been shown this letter before today? (No — only the words it sits inside.)
\end{tcolorbox}
